extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental scientists, and scholars interested in a method for discovering causes and building the sciences (readers of Bacon's Novum Organum)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for reconstructing natural philosophy by collecting, arranging, and reasoning from experiments and particulars; emphasizes new methods of induction, compiling natural history, and organisational practices to advance the sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare minds with hope and reasonable expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare and incline men's minds toward experiment by disclosing sound reasons for hope of success rather than merely criticizing the present state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inspiring despair by pointing out errors without offering grounds for hope; give concrete reasons (analogies like Columbus) to persuade cautious minds. Use hope as a motivational preparatory step while withholding unwarranted promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine experiment and reason (bee model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper method neither relies solely on empirical accumulation (ants) nor purely on abstract deduction (spiders) but combines gathered facts with active intellectual processing (the bee: collects and then works the matter with the understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be purely empirical (mere collection) or purely dogmatic (spinning theory from alone). Extract and transform experimental material with the intellect to produce useful axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue a pure, unmixed natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural philosophy must be cleared of corrupting influences from scholastic logic, misplaced natural theology, and inappropriate mathematical methods that terminate rather than generate natural philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting external theoretical systems (e.g., syllogistic logic or abstract metaphysics) dominate empirical inquiry; return to particulars and build philosophy from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish received theories and reapply the mind freshly to particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: One should be prepared to discard common theories and preconceived notions, and instead apply an unprejudiced, rigorous attention to particulars and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the tendency to reason from established theories; a mature, clear-sensed investigator should re-examine particulars afresh rather than fitting data to doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect a comprehensive natural history tailored to philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble a store of particulars (natural history) specifically compiled to serve as the foundation for deriving causes and axioms — not merely casual or literary compilations of species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural histories must be organized to inform the intellect (include mechanical experiments, commonplace phenomena, and details relevant to causal investigation). Distinguish histories compiled for curiosity from those intended as a basis for philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather 'enlightening' experiments (not only profitable ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect experiments that illuminate causes and axioms even if they have no immediate practical profit; such experiments are 'enlightening' because they decisively resolve questions about causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize experiments that reveal causal relations and never deceive on that aim; do not disregard experiments just because they are not commercially useful. Mechanicians' experiments must be harvested for their explanatory value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce a regular, ordered method of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience must be pursued according to a determined rule and order rather than by vague, arbitrary, or intermittent observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace groping and isolated observation with systematic programs of experiment and collection; establish procedures, sequencing, and sustained inquiry so results are cumulative and comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down and commit experiments to paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments and particulars must be recorded in writing rather than left to memory or informal transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure experiments are documented and accessible (written records enable compilation into natural histories and tables). Lack of written records hinders the use and verification of experimental material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange particulars into well-ordered 'tables of discovery'
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize collected particulars into prepared, digested tables that present the phenomena in ways that assist the understanding and enable systematic induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave particulars dispersed; put them in 'living tables' so the mind can apply itself to readymade, arranged material rather than skirmishing across unconnected facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed by successive ascent from particulars to axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason must ascend by a true scale: from particulars to lesser axioms, then to intermediate axioms, and only then to the most general — avoiding jumps from particulars to remote generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid syllogistic habits that leap directly to abstract universal principles. Build intermediate axioms (which are useful and 'alive') and use them as the reliable basis for broader generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject simple enumeration as induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction by mere enumeration of instances is puerile and unreliable; instead use a method that separates nature by proper rejections and exclusions and seeks sufficient negatives before affirming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer general truths from few obvious examples. Employ procedures that test across exclusions and negatives (the described Baconian method) rather than counting confirming instances alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate axioms by their capacity to point to new particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: When an axiom is proposed, test whether it extends beyond its originating instances by whether it predicts or points out new particulars — confirmation is through generating new observable facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept an axiom merely because it fits original cases; require that it helps discover or anticipate new phenomena, thereby proving its extent and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid division (schism) of sciences; aim to extend and reduce particulars into one natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever possible, extend natural philosophy and reduce particular sciences into it to prevent dismembering of the sciences which hinders progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek unifying intermediate axioms and integrated accounts; fragmentation into isolated disciplines obstructs the derivation of general, useful rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduce causes and axioms from experiments, then deduce effects from those axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper sequence is to derive causes/axioms from experiments and then obtain new effects and experiments from those causes, rather than inferring from effects alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not follow the empiric's pattern of producing experiments from experiments without interpreting their causes; aim for interpretation that yields predictive and generative principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and allow correction of early errors in experimental compilations
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial collections and experiments will contain mistakes and trivial errors, but these can and should be expunged later by discovery of causes and axioms; do not be deterred by minor false particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor mistakes (like typographical errors in printing) are fixable; only persistent or widespread errors undermine the project. Maintain scrupulous compilation but tolerate corrigible faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include common, mean, and even sordid particulars in natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit ordinary, lowly, or mean instances (and even filthy particulars) into natural history because their causes can be informative and yield valuable knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exclude mundane phenomena on grounds of dignity; the causes of common things often underlie rarer effects. Examples: putrid matter providing fragrant substances; trivial objects yielding fundamental causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experiments that 'afford light' over immediate profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Give priority to experiments that illuminate nature (provide explanatory light) rather than those that are immediately practical or profitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable theoretical insight may have no immediate material utility but can lead to vast subsequent benefits; value explanatory power and causal clarity above short-term gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and transfer experiments across arts (literate experience) but expect greater gains from axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferring experiments from one art to another (literate experience) can produce useful results, but more important discoveries will come from deducing axioms from well-arranged particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-application of known experiments for incremental gains, but focus resources on the longer path: compiling and reasoning to intermediate axioms that yield larger, more general effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize labor and employ division of work for compiling experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress depends on united labors, abundant leisure for some, and distribution of tasks (each performing a separate part) rather than crowds repeating the same work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement coordinated programs, succession of workers across ages, and division of tasks (collecting, organizing, interpreting) to accelerate development of natural history and axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act despite uncertainty — attempt experiments even for faint hopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where hope is faint or uncertain, make the experimental attempt: the risk of neglect is far worse than the loss of limited labor from failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not paralyze inquiry through excessive caution; modest attempts can seed vast eventual benefits. Weigh the small cost of failure against the large cost of inaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the understanding: cleanse prejudices and avoid sect-forming
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying the method, prepare the mind by removing prejudices and false anticipations; do not aim to found a sect or propound abstract universal theories prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid selling a new sectarian theory or promising universal principles; focus on preparing minds to receive methodical evidence and tables that will gradually produce reliable philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer intermediate axioms for practical human business
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate axioms — those between particulars and the most general — are the most solid, lively, and useful for human affairs and should be the primary targets of discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overvalue notional, abstract generalities that have no weight in practice. Seek axioms that are limited, testable, and useful for applications.
